newsitem.title: USA: Women exceed men in most management skills - study.
newsitem.headline: Women exceed men in most management skills - study.

text.p: Women do a better job than men in 28 of 31 key management categories, including keeping productivity high and generating ideas, but they do poorly at handling frustration, a new study reported on Wednesday.

This was a departure from traditional presumptions, which credit women with being nurturing team players at work but not with skills associated with top management, one of the study's authors told Reuters.

"Women have traditionally been given credit for being good in terms of intuitive skills ... and the study confirmed that they do do well and outperform men in that area," said Janet Irwin, who wrote the study distributed by the non-profit Foundation for Future Leadership.

"But the study also showed that women were even stronger in more logic-based skills like ... getting things done on time, producing high-quality work, generating ideas, problem-solving and planning," Irwin said.
Women were even with men in one area -- delegating responsibility -- and were behind in the ability to handle pressure and cope with their own frustration, the study said.
Irwin said only 2 percent of chief executive officers at major U.S. corporations were women, which means the study could be a "wake-up call for corporate America."
"If we're going to win the war for an improved economy, a strong economy, creating better jobs and more jobs, we're going to need women ... in those top slots," Irwin said.

The study did not aim to single out gender differences at the outset but rather to identify leadership abilities; clear differences between men and women became apparent as the data were analysed, she said.

The study reviewed 6,403 questionnaires dealing with 915 corporate workers; the workers themselves filled out the questionnaires, as did their supervisors, subordinates and peers. The proportion of men to women was 70 percent to 30 percent, about the same ratio as in the overall U.S. management workforce, Irwin said.

The 31 areas of management ability surveyed were broken down into seven categories: problem-solving, planning, controlling, managing self, managing relationships, leading and communicating. While women did better than men in 28 of the 31 and excelled by a wide margin in 25, they were behind in a key area that was not part of the study: self-promotion.

"Women, I think, have been raised traditionally to be good little girls and ... women translate that to mean, 'If I just do a good job, people will come around and notice me and give me rewards for it,' and that just isn't the case," Irwin said. "Women have to be more assertive in demanding recognition for their efforts."
